Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a gastrointestinal motility disorder that results from the reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus or oral cavity resulting in symptoms or complications. The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx. GERD affects quality of life and may cause erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma. GERD is a clinical diagnosis and is most effectively treated with proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs). Long-term use of PPIs is associated with bone fractures, chronic renal disease, acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile intestinal infection.

Gastroesophageal reflux (GER) in children is very common and refers to the involuntary passage of gastric contents into the esophagus. This is often physiological and managed conservatively. In contrast, GER disease (GERD) is a less common pathologic process causing troublesome symptoms, which may need medical management. Apart from abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, other factors that play a role in the pathogenesis of GERD include defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility and clearance, as well as anatomical defects of the lower esophageal reflux barrier such as hiatal hernia. The clinical manifestations of GERD in young children are varied and nonspecific prompting the necessity for careful diagnostic evaluation. Management should be targeted to the underlying aetiopathogenesis and to limit complications of GERD. The following review focuses on up-to-date information regarding of the pathogenesis, diagnostic evaluation and management of GERD in children.

Symptoms potentially attributable to gastroesophageal reflux disease are among those most commonly reported to primary care providers in the outpatient setting. In this review, we discuss clinical approaches to the evaluation and management of these symptoms, including proton pump inhibitor trials as well as specific indications or clinical settings that warrant referral to Gastroenterology specialists.

data.narrative: The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of stomach contents into the throat [18#0]. The condition happens when stomach contents flow back into the esophagus or mouth, which can lead to complications such as inflammation, narrowing of the esophagus, and Barrett esophagus, which can precede esophageal cancer [18#1][18#2]. In children, symptoms can be varied and nonspecific, making careful diagnosis important [19#3]. Factors that contribute to GERD include abnormal relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter, weakened esophageal lining defenses, impaired movement and clearance of the esophagus and stomach, and anatomical defects such as hiatal hernia [19#4][19#5]. Long-term use of proton-pump inhibitors, the main treatment for GERD, is associated with bone fractures, kidney disease, pneumonia, and intestinal infection by Clostridium difficile [18#6].

data.narrative: GERD's typical symptoms are heartburn and regurgitation of stomach contents into the throat [18#0]. It happens when stomach contents flow back into the esophagus or mouth, and it can lead to serious problems including inflammation of the esophagus, narrowing of the esophagus, and a condition called Barrett esophagus that can precede esophageal cancer [18#1][18#2]. Risk factors for GERD include a hiatal hernia, weakened esophageal defenses, and problems with how the esophagus and stomach move and clear contents [19#3][19#4]. Long-term use of the most common GERD medications, called proton-pump inhibitors, carries its own risks including bone fractures, kidney disease, pneumonia, and intestinal infection [18#5]. In children, reflux is common and often normal, but GERD is a less common and more serious form that causes troubling symptoms and needs careful evaluation [19#6][19#7]. GERD-related symptoms are among the most common reasons people visit primary care doctors [20#8]. The condition is listed in the medical genetics database under the name Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) [2], and the entity name Gastroesophageal Reflux also appears in the literature [3]. Several research publications carry the title Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease [1][6][9][15]. One publication focuses on what is new in pediatric GERD under the title Gastroesophageal reflux disease in children: What's new right now? [12]. Clinical trials have studied treatments including famotidine for non-erosive GERD [4], pantoprazole for acid reflux symptoms in adults [7], on-demand treatment [13], and endoscopic fundoplication [16]. A study examining the natural history of gastroesophageal reflux in children and adolescents has also been conducted [10]. Additional publications on GERD are identified by PMID 29132520 [5], PMID 33351044 [8], PMID 36170502 [11], PMID 37034973 [14], and PMID 37516506 [17].
